GeoInv3D · field-data test · 27 September 2026

Karnataka Gravity Depth Diagnosis

Analysis of the sparse inversion run on AWS EC2: data fit, the recovered density model, why the model extends to the bottom of the mesh, a comparison of αs, norms, depth weighting and L1–L2, and an independent cross-check against Tomofast-x (gravity only).

Area
70 × 70 km, easting 641–711 km, northing 1634–1704 km (UTM 43N, EPSG:32643)
Data
NGPM Bouguer anomaly, 500 m grid decimated to 1 km: 5040 points; second-order trend surface removed
Mesh
1 km × 1 km × 500 m core, 10 km deep, 20 km padding (factor 1.3): 84 × 84 × 27 = 190,512 cells
Runs
AWS EC2 ap-south-1: sparse on c5.2xlarge (4.6 min), L1–L2 on c5.4xlarge (3.5 min); 15-run parameter study run locally; 4 checks on the 1 km mesh on 28 September (2 submitted from the upload page); SimPEG vs Tomofast-x on an 8 km deep mesh on 24 September

Summary

  • The data fit is fine. χ²/N = 0.97, residual RMS 0.49 mGal, correlation between observed and predicted data 0.9986.
  • The model has no vertical resolution. Below the core area the share of |mass| per 500 m layer barely changes from the surface to 10 km (2.9% → 2.3%); 50% of the anomalous mass lies in the padding below 10 km (D50 = 9.1 km). The power spectrum of the residual anomaly puts the sources at 1.1, 2.2 and 6.0 km.
  • The main cause is αs = 10⁻⁴. The pipeline passes αx,y,z as length scales, so SimPEG weights the gradient terms by (1 × 500 m)²; per cell the smallness term is about 2500 times weaker, and its compactness (ps = 0) has almost no effect. With an L1 vertical gradient (pz = 1), a column that is constant with depth costs almost nothing. Changing only the depth weighting, with αs unchanged, leaves the result as it was.
  • αs = 1 with Li & Oldenburg depth weighting removes the columns. On the 2 km mesh (β = 1), the share of mass inside the core rises from 25% to 80%, the lateral padding share falls from 26% to 5%, D50 = 4.6 km, and the fit is unchanged. A smaller β gives a shallower model; the classic β = 2 is deeper here.
  • L1–L2 is equally compact. At full resolution on EC2: 80% of the mass in the core, D50 = 3.0 km, strongest positive body (north-west) at 0.75–2.25 km.
  • The full-resolution check confirms this. On the 1 km mesh with αs = 1, the dense body under the main Bouguer high lies at 2.3–4.8 / 3.3–7.8 / 4.3–11.1 km for β = 0.5 / 1 / 1.5, with nearly the same fit (χ²/N 0.86–0.96). β = 0.5 and L1–L2 give the same depth. At the same place, the 2 km study predicted the base of the body to within 0.5 km (Section 7).
  • Cross-check with Tomofast-x. On 24 September both codes inverted the same gravity data on the same 8 km deep mesh. SimPEG (αs = 0.05, chi 1.04) gave a dense body closed at the top and the bottom, at 3.3–7.3 km (half maximum) under the main Bouguer high, which agrees with this report's full-resolution αs = 1, β = 1 run (3.3–7.8 km); that mesh reached 14.4 km, so the base is not the mesh floor. Tomofast-x fitted the data more closely (chi 0.65) but its model is nearly the same from the surface to the mesh floor, with no base, and it took about 2.7 hours against SimPEG's 9 minutes (Section 8).
  • Caveat. Gravity data alone do not determine depth; the regularization does. "Shallower" here means the model is no longer pushed to the bottom of the mesh. The actual depths need constraints from rock densities, geological sections or seismic data.

1Data and preprocessing

Within the area the Bouguer anomaly ranges from -94.9 to -44.3 mGal. Its main feature is a NW–SE trending high from (650, 1685) to (675, 1660) km. The second-order trend surface (regional field) ranges from -95.3 to -75.9 mGal; removing it lowers the standard deviation of the data from 9.99 to 9.35 mGal and leaves a residual of -16.4 to +31.7 mGal. Every point was given an error of 0.5 mGal (noise floor).

Sign convention. Bouguer data are positive downward (positive over dense rock), while SimPEG's gz is positive upward. Before these runs the pipeline was fixed accordingly: the data are multiplied by −1 before SimPEG, and the observed and predicted data in the result are returned in the original convention. Without the fix, field data invert to a density model of the wrong sign.

2Inversion settings

Regularization
sparse (IRLS), norms p = [ps, px, py, pz] = [0, 2, 2, 1]
Weights
αs = 10⁻⁴, αx = αy = αz = 1 (length scales)
Depth weighting
SimPEG sensitivity weighting (UpdateSensitivityWeights)
Bounds
−0.2 to +0.5 g/cc density contrast (rock samples 2.52–3.40 g/cc, median 2.66)
Choice of β
χ² = N (DampedUpdateIRLS); at most 30 iterations and 30 IRLS iterations
Mesh
84 × 84 × 27 cells with a 70 × 70 × 20 core; the 7 bottom padding layers are 650 m to 3.1 km thick, and the mesh ends at about 22 km depth

3Convergence and data fit

The target φd = N = 5040 was reached at iteration 16; the following IRLS iterations kept φd between 4770 and 4895, ending at φd = 4895 (χ²/N = 0.97). During iterations 5–15 φd stayed near 5500 with β unchanged while IRLS adjusted the sparsity weights.

Residual RMS is 0.49 mGal, the largest residual 7.7 mGal, and 5.8% of the points have |residual / σ| > 2. The normalized residuals are not Gaussian: a sharp central peak with long tails. Most smooth areas are fitted better than the error level (over-fitting), while isolated spikes remain (single points in the residual map, Figure 3), most likely outliers from the original gridding. We suggest removing them, or using a robust (L1) misfit, before the next run; a 0.5 mGal noise floor may also be too small for gridded data.

4The recovered density model

The model reproduces the main structures in the data: a NW–SE dense belt (up to +0.19 g/cc) and several parallel low-density belts to the east (down to -0.16 g/cc). The dense belt follows the regional structural trend and may correspond to a schist or greenstone belt; this should be checked against the geological map.

The problem is the vertical direction. The depth slices at 0.3, 2.3, 5.3 and 9.8 km are almost identical (Figure 4), and at 14.9 km, in the padding, the pattern is the same, only smoother. In the sections (Figure 5) every anomaly is a column from the surface to the bottom of the mesh. The half-maximum extent of the strongest positive anomaly is 0.25–8.3 km, and that of the strongest negative anomaly 0.25–6.8 km.

5Why the model extends downward

In numbers

Core / lateral padding / below 10 km
24% / 26% / 50% of |density contrast × volume|
Depth distribution below the core area
D50 = 9.1 km, D90 = 17.6 km; 72% below 5 km
Spectral depth estimates
deep 6.0 km, intermediate 2.2 km, shallow 1.1 km (Spector & Grant, Figure 6)

Causes

  1. The compactness term does not act. The pipeline passes αx,y,z to SimPEG as length scales, so the gradient terms are weighted by (length scale × smallest cell)² = (1 × 500 m)² = 2.5 × 10⁵. With the 1/h² of the gradient (h = 1000 m) this is about 0.25 Δm² per cell, against 10⁻⁴ m² for the smallness term, about 2500 times weaker. The sparse (compactness) constraint ps = 0 therefore has almost no effect, and the inversion is in effect driven by the smoothness terms.
  2. L1 on the vertical gradient. pz = 1 favours models that are piecewise constant with depth. A column that does not change with depth has zero vertical gradient and costs almost nothing, so it can extend to the bottom of the mesh.
  3. Sensitivity weighting makes the padding cheap. The weights follow the data's sensitivity to each cell; padding cells outside the area and at depth have low sensitivity and therefore low weights, so mass placed there costs little. 26% of the mass went into the lateral padding.

Cause 1 dominates: switching only the depth weighting to Li & Oldenburg (base_dw1), with αs still 10⁻⁴, gives almost the same result (49% below 10 km), whereas αs = 1 alone brings the share below 10 km down to 22%.

6Parameter study

For a quick comparison, 15 sparse inversions were run locally on a 2 km × 2 km × 1 km mesh (every fourth point, 1295 data), about 25 s each. The baseline (original settings) reproduces the full-resolution result (D50 8.7 km versus 9.1 km; 50% below 10 km in both), so the coarse runs show the right trends. Depth weighting is the new option depth_weighting: "depth": the model-norm weight is (z + z₀)−β/2, where z is the depth below the stations and z₀ half the smallest cell.

Core, lateral padding and below 10 km add up to 100%. Red cells: lateral padding > 20%, below 10 km > 30% or D50 > 7 km. The last two columns give the peak of the strongest positive anomaly and its half-maximum depth range; +0.50 means the upper bound was reached.

Observations

  • αs decides whether the model reaches the bottom. With αs = 10⁻⁴ or 10⁻², 45–50% of the mass lies below 10 km; with αs = 1 about 20%.
  • Depth weighting decides the lateral leakage and the mean depth. With αs = 1 and p = [0,2,2,2], sensitivity weighting leaves 33% in the lateral padding; depth weighting only 5–10%.
  • β sets the mean depth. β = 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 / 2 give D50 = 1.9 / 4.6 / 6.8 / 8.9 km. The D50 for β = 1 is close to the deep spectral estimate (6.0 km); β = 0.5 is closer to the intermediate and shallow estimates.
  • The norms matter less. With αs = 1 and β = 1, p = [0,2,2,2], [0,2,2,1] and [0,1,1,1] all give D50 of 4.6–5.4 km.
  • Bounds. With αs = 1 the main bodies reach the +0.5 / −0.2 g/cc bounds, i.e. blocky and saturated. αs = 0.1 with β = 1 peaks at +0.29 g/cc without saturating, with the anomaly at 0.5–4.5 km, which is a sound compromise.

7Full-resolution check

On 28 September four more sparse inversions were run on the same 1 km mesh as the original run (190,512 cells; p = [0,2,2,2], density contrast in [−0.2, 0.5] g/cc, depth weighting depth); the β = 0.5 and 1.5 runs were submitted from the upload page as a parameter sweep. The table also lists the original settings and L1–L2. Depths are read from the density profiles under the main Bouguer high (easting 671.5 km, northing 1664.5 km) and the north-western high (650.5, 1682.5 km).

Observations

  • The columns are gone. With depth weighting the main body ends above 12 km in every run; with the original settings it reached the bottom of the mesh (19.9 km).
  • β sets the depth, and the data cannot tell. From β = 0.5 to 1 to 1.5 the peak of the main body moves from 3.8 km to 6.8 km and 9.3 km, while χ²/N stays between 0.86 and 0.96. This is the non-uniqueness of gravity inversion: choosing β needs independent depth information.
  • β = 0.5 agrees with L1–L2. Two quite different regularizations both put the main body at 2.3–4.8 km, near the intermediate spectral estimate (2.2 km); the 6.8 km of β = 1 is close to the deep estimate (6.0 km).
  • The 2 km study predicted this well. At the same place the 2 km mesh gave 0.5–4.5 / 3.5–7.5 / 4.5–10.6 km for β = 0.5 / 1 / 1.5: the base within 0.5 km of the 1 km mesh, the top and the peak 1–3 km shallower.
  • β = 1.5 starts to trail to depth. The low-density body in the east reaches 20 km, and 33% of the mass lies below 10 km.

8Independent cross-check: SimPEG and Tomofast-x

On 24 September the same Karnataka gravity data were inverted with two independent codes: SimPEG, used throughout this project, and Tomofast-x 2.0, an open-source parallel code, as a cross-check. Both used the same 8 km deep mesh (500 m horizontal and 250 m vertical cells), the same cloud machine (16 vCPU, 123 GB memory) and the same noise model. Only the gravity part is summarised here; for magnetics see the original report (Desktop/Tomofastx_vs_SimPEG_package).

SimPEGTomofast-x 2.0
Data fit, chi1.040.65
Data used4,900 points (every second node)19,600 points (all)
Body under the main Bouguer high3.3–7.3 km at half maximum, peak 0.64 g/cc at 5.0 km; 0.03 g/cc at 9.2 km, while the mesh reaches 14.4 kmNo base: the 1st, 50th and 99th percentiles of each layer change by less than 10% from the surface to 8 km
RegularizationChosen once: sparse, norms (0, 2, 2, 1), αs = 0.05, sensitivity-based depth weighting24-trial search of two smoothing weights; still no shape
Time to the final model9 minutes (522 s)About 2.7 hours (1.7 h search + 1.0 h full run)

How it relates to this report

  • Why the 24 September SimPEG model has a base. It used αs = 0.05. With length-scale alphas the smallness term is then about a fifth of the gradient terms, so the compactness constraint acts; this report's "original settings" used αs = 10⁻⁴, about 2500 times weaker, and gave columns. This is the diagnosis of Section 5.
  • Two independent set-ups give the same depth. The 8 km mesh (octree, 500 m cells, sensitivity depth weighting) gives 3.3–7.3 km; the 1 km tensor mesh with αs = 1 and Li & Oldenburg β = 1 gives 3.3–7.8 km (Figure 12). β = 0.5 and L1–L2 are shallower (2.3–4.8 km) and β = 1.5 deeper (4.3–11.1 km); the data cannot tell these apart (Section 7).
  • A good chi is not evidence of a good model. Tomofast-x reached chi 0.65, below the target, with no vertical shape at all; this report's β sweep also shows models with nearly the same chi whose depths differ by a factor of two. A settings search that looks only at chi selects physically meaningless settings. A published Tomofast-x application (Bird et al., 2025, Antarctic bathymetry) reached the same conclusion and ran 72 full-length trial inversions instead.

Cost (gravity only)

StageApprox. time
SimPEG gravity, final run (8 km mesh, 16 vCPU)9 minutes (522 s)
Tomofast-x gravity: 24-trial settings search1.7 hours
Tomofast-x gravity: full-length run1.0 hour
SimPEG (this report, EC2 c5.2xlarge, 1 km mesh)5–6 minutes per run, about $0.03

Most of Tomofast-x's cost comes from one feature: it does not tune its own regularization, so its two smoothing weights must be found before a run by repeated trials, each 12–17 minutes on the full problem. SimPEG adjusts β during the run and needs no search.

What this does not show

  • SimPEG used less data: 4,900 points against Tomofast-x's 19,600. Tomofast-x handles the full data volume with a wavelet-compressed sensitivity matrix, a real strength this comparison does not credit.
  • SimPEG had its own problems: two faults in the workflow at the time (a mesh-depth setting that had no effect, a missing solver speed-up) took hours to find. They are fixed, but the time is not in the table.
  • Tomofast-x can converge here: on a shallower 3 km mesh it reached an on-target fit (gravity chi 1.87) with a search. The failure is in producing a bounded body at depth, not in fitting the data.
  • We may not have used Tomofast-x well: its published applications also use bound constraints and other controls that we did not try. Its smoothness term cannot be made "blocky" as SimPEG's can, our best explanation for the copied-downward pattern, but that is a hypothesis and was not tested further.
  • One dataset, one operator: a single survey handled by one person new to Tomofast-x.

9Recommendations and next steps

  1. Sparse settings: αs = 1 (now the pipeline default), p = [0,2,2,2] or [0,2,2,1], depth weighting depth with β between 0.5 and 1: β = 0.5 agrees with L1–L2, β = 1 with the deep spectral estimate. Report this range of depths rather than a single model.
  2. Fix the depth with independent data: use rock densities, geological sections, boreholes or seismic data to constrain the top and base of the main dense body, and choose β accordingly. The upload page's parameter sweep submits several β at once and compares them in one workflow.
  3. Handle the spikes in the data: remove isolated outliers or use a robust misfit, and check whether the 0.5 mGal noise floor is appropriate.
  4. Add prior information: density bounds by lithology or a reference model; geological sections or seismic data to constrain depth. A joint inversion with the available aeromagnetic TMI data is another option.
  5. Mesh: the bottom padding cells are thick (up to 3.1 km) and absorb mass. The pipeline's mesh recommendation (2 km cells, 35 km deep core) suits deeper targets; for the upper crust, a 10 km core with depth weighting is enough.
  6. Tomofast-x: worth considering where SimPEG exceeds memory even after thinning, or for joint gravity–magnetic inversion. If it is used, run full-length trials (not short proxies), check the recovered depth profile and not chi alone, and run no more than two magnetic-size trials at a time on a 123 GB machine.
  7. L1–L2 solver: the coordinate-descent solver of Utsugi (2019) is too slow at 190,000 cells (single-threaded; each λ point took about twice as long as the previous one, 11 of 41 points in 11 minutes). This run used IRLS on the same elastic-net objective and finished in 3.5 minutes.
